description_full: MVB Financial Corp. operates as bank holding company for MVB Bank, Inc that provides financial services to individuals and corporate clients. The company operates through three segments: CoRe Banking, Mortgage Banking, and Financial Holding Company. It offers various demand deposit accounts, savings accounts, money market accounts, and certificates of deposit; and commercial, consumer, and real estate mortgage loans, as well as lines of credit. The company provides debit cards; cashier's checks; safe deposit rental facilities; and non-deposit investment services, as well as financial technology (Fintech) banking services. In addition, it offers fintech solutions for the gaming, payments, banking-as-a-service, and digital asset sectors; fraud prevention services for merchants, credit agencies, Fintech companies, and other vendors; and digital products and web and mobile applications for forward-thinking community banks, credit unions, digital banks, and Fintech companies. It operates full-service branches in West Virginia and Virginia. The company was founded in 1999 and is based in Fairmont, West Virginia.

financial_summary: MVB Financial Corp. is a micro-cap financial services business with a $296M market cap on $168M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 11% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $2M in free cash flow — roughly 1 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.15×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 0.5× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 6.4% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 10% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.
